title: The wild elephant tamed
hookLine: the mind trained like a forest elephant tied to a post

lines: THE BUDDHA TELLS AN ELEPHANT STORY.
cards: A young novice named Aciravata is living in a quiet forest hut near Rajagaha. Prince Jayasena comes walking by and asks him a question: is it true that a monk can make the mind truly one-pointed?
The novice explains it as best he can. The prince listens, says that's impossible, and walks away. Aciravata goes to the Buddha and tells him what happened.
How could a prince who lives for pleasure understand that? the Buddha says. And then he tells a story about elephants.

teach.h: THE ONE AT THE FOOT OF THE MOUNTAIN
teach.b: First a picture: two friends at the foot of a mountain. One climbs, and from the top sees parks, groves and lakes. The other, still at the bottom, says: what you see is impossible.
He's not lying. The mountain is in the way. Then the elephant.
A king tells his elephant tamer to catch a wild forest elephant.

teach.h: TIED TO A POST, SPOKEN TO GENTLY
teach.b: The tamer plants a great post in the ground and binds the elephant's neck to it, to wear away its forest habits, its forest memories, its distress at leaving the forest, and to make it comfortable around people.
Then he speaks to it gently, words pleasant to hear. When the elephant listens, he gives it grass and water.

teach.h: PICK IT UP, PUT IT DOWN
teach.b: Then simple training: pick this up, put this down. Then harder: stand firm when struck, stay steady in noise. Until at last the elephant is worthy of a king.
The posts, the Buddha says, are the four foundations of mindfulness. They tie the mind so its old restless, grasping habits can wear away.
Even after deep stillness, he adds one more step: don't think thoughts tied to desire, and later, not even thoughts at all; just rest.
Notice the pace: a post, gentle words and food, small tasks first; the hard tests come last. The mind, in this picture, isn't an enemy.
It's a strong, wild creature that can learn, slowly, to stand still.

how: Some meditation teachers describe returning to the breath as tying the mind to a post, and a well-known Tibetan painting of the stages of calm shows taming the mind as an elephant that slowly turns from dark to white along a path.

o: the tamed state, a mind trained slowly and gently
a mind broken by force and harsh punishment
a wild mind left free to roam where it likes

games.q: the wild elephant tamed: tap the pairs.
p: the young novice in the forest

s: the elephant tamer in MN 125 starts by beating the elephant into obedience
he starts by tying it to a post, speaking gently, feeding it, and teaching small things first.
the Buddha uses a picture of two friends and a mountain
the one at the bottom can't see what the climber sees, so he calls it impossible.
the posts in the simile stand for the four foundations of mindfulness
they tie the mind so old habits can wear away.

games.q: you've caught a wild forest elephant and tied it to a post. it's restless and distressed. what does the tamer do next?
o: leave it alone until it gives up.
speak to it gently, then give food and water when it listens.
send it back to the forest.
games.why: the tamer uses pleasant words, then food and water, then small steps. the training is slow and patient.

practice: Let the breath be the post. The mind will pull, the way a forest elephant pulls, and that's expected; each time it wanders, bring it back with a kind word in your own head, like the tamer's: here, back to the post.

wordCard.voice: Dantabhumi. The tamed state: the mind tied to the four foundations of mindfulness like a forest elephant to a post, trained with gentle words and small steps.

orig.note: Pali dantabhumi: the tamed state, the ground of the tamed. the title of MN 125.

carryVoice: Your line: tamed slowly. Gentle words come first, and the hard tests last. That's day four ninety-four.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 125, Dantabhumi Sutta (the grade of the tamed)
